name: Cookie syncing
plain: Ad companies swap IDs through redirects so each can recognise the same person.
meaning: Vendor A redirects the browser to vendor B with its own ID in the URL, so B stores a mapping A to B. Repeated across dozens of partners it builds the ID graph that real time bidding relies on. Academic crawls found it on a large share of sites.

web.api: Image or iframe request to partner /sync?uid=...; 302 redirects; postMessage

access.persistence: Mapping tables persist at vendors for months to years
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

firefox.note: Partitioned so syncs are siloed per site

safari.note: Blocked, uses link decoration or login IDs

data.update: per page view with partner tags

limits.headline: Can let ad companies swap IDs so each recognizes you across sites
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page loads ads or trackers
can: Pass your IDs between ad companies through quick redirects
Match your visits across many sites
Build one profile from several companies' cookies
cannot: Work where third party cookies are blocked, as in Safari and Firefox by default
Know your name without a login or an email hash
Work between browsers or devices unless a login links them
limits.differs: Safari and Firefox block most of this by default. Chrome still allows third party cookies.

story.what_it_is: Ad companies swap IDs through quick redirects so each can recognise the same person.
story.for_you: You never see it. When you load a page, your browser is sent through several ad companies in a blink. Each one passes along its ID for you, so they can all say that they know you.
story.for_makers: Real time ad auctions need every bidder to know who is on the page. Syncing lets them match their private IDs with each other. The result is a web of IDs that makes ads follow people, and a large share of sites take part.

use_cases.example: A news page loads, and a dozen ad companies swap IDs so they can bid on you within 100 milliseconds.
A measurement company uses synced IDs to count people who saw an ad on one site and bought on another.
A free browser game loads ads through partners that sync IDs so bidders value a player more.
A video site sells ad space with synced IDs, which raises the price for known viewers.
A shopper's cart visit is shared through synced IDs so a related ad shows on a news site.
Researchers studied syncing to show how many sites share one ID.

risks: Builds a web of IDs that follows you

technical_bounds: Needs a third-party cookie or another stable ID on each side
Blocked by Safari ITP and Firefox TCP; Chrome allows it with third-party cookies on
Browsers cannot distinguish a sync from an ordinary pixel

abuse: Cross-vendor profile merging without the person knowing

history.change: Papadopoulos et al. (WWW 2019) quantified cookie syncing in the wild

refs.label: Cookie Synchronization: Everything You Always Wanted to Know (WWW 2019)
